label: DAILY EDITION
title: Three things worth knowing
subtitle: A promising Phase II skin-disease result, record little-tern nesting and new AI safeguards for workers.

stories.title: Phase II skin-disease trial reached a 72% response rate
stories.text: In Merck’s mid-stage trial, 72% of patients receiving the highest tulisokibart dose achieved at least a 50% reduction in inflammatory lesions after 16 weeks, compared with 35% on placebo. Forty-one percent achieved at least a 75% reduction, versus 15% on placebo.
stories.why: The result points to a potential new treatment for hidradenitis suppurativa, a chronic condition that causes painful skin lumps. Tulisokibart remains experimental, and larger trials must confirm its effectiveness and long-term safety.

stories.title: Little-tern breeding pairs doubled to a record 126 at Long Nanny
stories.text: At least 126 little-tern pairs nested at the protected Northumberland site—double its previous record—and at least 82 chicks fledged. The rebound followed years of disruption from bird flu, flooding and extreme weather.
stories.why: The season shows that careful protection of a vulnerable breeding site can produce measurable recovery. It is one season at one site, and other English tern colonies still recorded declines.

stories.title: California barred employers from relying on AI to fire workers
stories.text: Newly signed laws also ban employers from using biometric data to predict workers’ emotions and require written notice when AI is responsible for mass layoffs.
stories.why: The measures establish concrete worker protections as AI spreads through employment decisions. They apply only in California, and their effectiveness will depend on implementation and enforcement.
